# Will an Off-Center Steering Wheel Be Corrected in an Alignment Visit?

Installing an OEM heated steering wheel on a 2016 Volvo XC90 presents a specific mechanical challenge distinct from simply bolting on an accessory part. The concern is valid: if the new wheel mounts slightly off-center relative to the steering shaft, will a standard wheel alignment fix this issue? The short answer is no, and understanding why requires looking past the suspension geometry that defines a "alignment" visit into the internal mechanics of the steering rack and column.

A standard four-wheel alignment adjusts the angles of the tires contacting the roadâcamber, caster, and toeâto ensure predictable handling and even tire wear. While the Volvo XC90 utilizes electric power-assisted rack-and-pinion steering, which eliminates hydraulic fluid concerns, the fundamental linkage between the wheels and the steering column remains rigid. The adjustment bolts on the tie rods set the lateral position of the wheels relative to each other, but they do not control the rotational orientation of the steering wheel itself.

If you mount a new steering wheel and it sits 2 o'clock or 4 o'clock off-center while the vehicle is driving straight, an alignment technician cannot rotate the wheel back to center using the standard equipment. Alignment stands measure caster, camber, and toe by monitoring the position of the wheels. They do not have direct access to the internal spline of the steering column where the wheel attaches. Even if you manually rotate the wheel to the "12 o'clock" position while driving straight and lock it there, the underlying misalignment between the wheel's mounting point and the rack's centerline persists.

The root cause usually lies in how the new wheel was installed or a slight variation in the spline engagement depth. When the wheel is bolted onto the splined shaft, if it isn't rotated to the absolute center mark during installation, that offset becomes permanent unless you can remove the wheel and rotate it further. Once the bolts are torqued to specification, the wheel is fixed in that rotational position relative to the rack's input.

Consider this scenario: You drive the car straight at 45 mph. The vehicle tracks perfectly with no pull to the left or right. However, your hands are resting at the 3 and 9 o'clock positions, yet the steering wheel itself is rotated so the top is pointing at 1 o'clock. This indicates an offset between the wheel's mounting interface and the center of the rack. An alignment visit will verify that the toe settings are correct (the wheels are pointing straight), but it cannot mechanically rotate the column to align the wheel face with the vehicle's forward axis.

The only way to correct this is to remove the steering wheel, rotate it on the shaft until the desired position matches the center of the rack's travel, and reinstall it. You must ensure that when you install the wheel, the stop pins or detents (if present) are engaged correctly, or simply tighten the retaining nut while holding the wheel in the perfect center position relative to the steering shaft.

It is important not to confuse this with a "centering" adjustment often found on older hydraulic systems where a cable could be adjusted under the dash. Modern electric power-steering units like those in the XC90 generally lack these external adjustment points. The centering is purely determined by the physical assembly of the wheel onto the column.

If you proceed with the installation, take care to align the wheel visually or mechanically against the rack's neutral position before tightening the retaining nut. Relying on an alignment shop to fix a rotational offset is a common misconception that leads to frustration and unnecessary service visits. The solution lies in the initial installation torque sequence and positioning, not in the suspension geometry settings.
